One cup, he said, would be Daniel's from lunch, and the other perhaps from his tea, for Daniel never washed up before the end of the day. It was a perfectly sensible answer, and it was delivered with a smoothness that Marianne noted without knowing why.

Pell closed her notebook and said that she would treat Daniel as a missing person from now on, and she asked Owen to telephone her at once if his friend came back. Owen offered Marianne a lift home in his blue van, but she thanked him and said that she would rather walk. She went out into the dark street and turned toward the harbour, where the clock tower stood like a pale finger against the night.

Marianne let herself into her cottage on Chapel Row, where her cat Biscuit met her at the door with an air of grave reproach, and she fed him before she thought of herself. The kettle boiled and the toast went cold, and she could not eat a mouthful. All the time her eyes kept straying to the telephone on the dresser, which stayed obstinately silent.

When the cat had settled, she spread Daniel's folder on the kitchen table beneath the lamp and began to read her notes of the past eight months. There were not many pages, and most of them recorded little more than the date, the weather and the word silent in her own small, tidy hand. She read them slowly, as one reads old letters, hoping to be surprised by some small thing she had missed.

She was surprised at the third session, where a single line had been underlined twice in her own pencil. Anna's red scarf, it said, was never found, and Daniel had told no one else. She had understood then how much trust it cost him to say it, but not how much it might matter.

She could hear him still, in that flat, unhurried voice, listing what the police had returned to him as if he were reading a catalogue: his sister's coat, her bag, her purse and her watch. They had never given him the scarf, a long red one that he himself had given her for her birthday and that she wore on every cold evening. When he had asked, they had told him that it had probably been washed out to sea.

She drew a small scarf in the margin of the page, looked at it, and frowned. A scarf floats; the harbour had given back everything else that Anna carried; and the police had searched the quay and the steps, so somebody must know where it went. The thought was cold and simple, and she found it almost impossible to put out of her mind.

Her thoughts returned, uninvited, to Owen Marsh, with his good coat and his damp hands and his perfectly reasonable explanations. She told herself that the man had done nothing but be kind, that a worried friend might well hurry into a shop, and that a counselor above all people ought not to leap to conclusions. And yet the unease would not leave her, like a note played slightly out of tune.

At midnight she dialled Daniel's number once more, and once more she heard it ring and ring in some distant room until the machine took over. She put the phone down on the table very gently, as though it might break, and went up to bed with the cat. Sleep, when it came at all, came in thin, restless pieces, and she woke each time to the sound of the wind in the chimney.

Saturday dawn spread grey and cold over the roofs of Saltmere, and the first gulls began to wheel and cry above the harbour. Marianne stood at her bedroom window with a cup of tea she did not want and looked across the town to the clock tower, whose great white face told her, quite correctly, that it was ten minutes past seven. She felt a foolish relief, as if that steady dial were a promise that nothing could go too far wrong.

At eight she telephoned Pell, who had no news of Daniel and sounded as though she had slept no more than Marianne had. Marianne took a breath, said that he had not come back and that she had been given something to keep for him, and told Pell about the brass key and the locker at the railway station. There was a short silence on the line, and then Pell said that she would meet her there in half an hour.

The railway station was crowded with Saturday travellers, children, suitcases and bicycles, and the echoing hall smelled of coffee and wet umbrellas. Marianne pushed through the crowd with the key tight in her fist, and found Pell waiting beside the lockers in her grey raincoat, with a pair of thin gloves already in her hand. They exchanged a brief nod, and neither of them wasted a word on greetings or on the weather.

Rows of green metal lockers stood in the echoing hall like the cells of a great beehive, each one bearing its number in white paint. They walked the length of the first row and half of the second before they found the one they wanted, at the very end, beneath a flickering lamp. Marianne's hand was not quite steady as she lifted the key and fitted it into the little lock.

The brass key turned smoothly, and the little door swung open with a squeak that seemed to echo around the whole station. Inside, on an otherwise empty shelf, sat a plain grey cardboard box tied up with string, and nothing else at all. It looked so ordinary that for a moment Marianne felt almost foolish, as though she had expected something grander.

Pell drew on a pair of thin gloves, lifted the box out as carefully as if it were full of eggs, and weighed it in her hands. She did not open it in the hall, where any passing stranger might look over her shoulder, but carried it straight out to her car. Marianne followed, feeling that she had stepped from a quiet counselor's room into a world with sharper edges.

Pell's office was on the second floor of the police station, a plain room with a barred window, a battered desk and a mug of cold coffee. She cleared a space on the table, cut the string, and unpacked the box with the slow precision of a person defusing a bomb. It held a green account book, a small leather diary with a brass clasp, and a brown envelope fastened with a rubber band.

She opened the account book at the first page, where the name Anna Reeve was written inside the cover in a clear, schoolgirl hand. It was the record that Anna had kept for the family business, Marsh and Reeve Clocks, where she had come every Thursday to put the books in order. Every entry was neat, and every column had been ruled with a pencil and a straight edge.

Pell's finger moved slowly down the columns of dates, descriptions and prices, and she began to read aloud in a low voice. Over two years, about thirty antique watches had been sold, gold and silver, each of them without any papers, and the last of them only a few days before Anna died. The sums were large enough to matter to a small shop and small enough to pass unnoticed.

Beside every sale, in the column headed seller, stood the same two initials, D and R. Pell read them out one by one, in the same level tone, and with each repetition Marianne felt a little colder, as though the room were slowly filling with winter. She did not need Pell to tell her whose initials they were, and she did not want to hear it said.

Pell sat back, folded her hands, and said in a grave voice that they had to consider the possibility that Daniel Reeve was a thief, and that he had run away. It would explain, she went on, why a man should give away a key and vanish, and perhaps what his sister had discovered. Marianne was shaken, because she could not believe it, and yet she knew how little she really knew of him.

Looking more closely, Marianne noticed tiny pencil marks in the margin beside three of the sales, so faint that they might have been taken for smudges. In Anna's small neat hand they asked whether the writing really belonged to Daniel, and the question seemed to hang in the air above the page. Pell admitted that it was curious, but said that it might mean almost anything, even that Anna was checking his spelling.

From the brown envelope Pell drew a small printed card, cream-coloured and slightly bent, which read Lunt and Daughter, Antique Watches, Carrow. It was the name of a dealer in a town forty minutes away by train, and it had been tucked in among the papers as if someone wished it to be found. The dealer was away at a trade fair until Sunday, said Pell, so she would call on him herself the next day.

Pell opened the little leather diary, which had a brass clasp that Anna had never locked, and began to read aloud from the last autumn of her life. Her voice was dry and careful, the voice of a woman who had learned that the dead deserve to be read slowly. Marianne listened, and the small round handwriting seemed to speak in a young, clear voice of its own.

Anna wrote that she kept the books for Marsh and Reeve Clocks on Thursdays, and that she loved the quiet of the workroom, with its ticking and its smell of oil and brass. She mentioned Daniel humming under his breath over his tiny wheels while she added up the sums for the week. Each entry was cheerful, ordinary and warm, and Marianne found it harder to hear than a tragedy.

In September, however, the tone began to change, and Anna wrote that she had noticed something strange in the stock book. Several watches that customers had left for repair were marked as sold, and there was nothing to show who had sold them, when, or to whom. She had checked the shelves twice, she wrote, and the watches were certainly not there.

Anna set down a small, precise observation that struck Marianne at once: Daniel always signed his work with his full name and a tiny clock hand drawn beside it, like a seal. The signatures on the sales were only the two letters, D and R, with no clock hand at all. Someone, she wrote carefully, was using her brother's name and had not troubled to copy his habits.

The last page was dated the Wednesday before she died, and it was shorter than the others. She wrote that she dreaded Friday, but that she must be fair, and that she would ask O to explain, because she owed him that chance before she told Daniel. After that the diary was blank, and the white pages seemed louder than the writing.

Pell closed the diary and tapped it slowly with one finger, frowning at the wall as though it might offer a better reading. O could mean anyone, she said at last, a friend, a customer, a tradesman or none of them, and yet she admitted that it was odd that Anna should have dreaded a Friday and died on it. She did not say that it was proof of anything, and Marianne did not ask her to.

She rose and stood at the window with her back to the room, and told Marianne, almost to herself, how the first case had been closed. The harbour steps were green with weed, the tide had been high, there was no mark on Anna and no witness who had seen her fall. It had looked so much like an accident that she had put her doubts aside, and she had never quite forgiven herself.

Marianne looked down at her hands, folded tightly in her lap, and felt the weight of the one thing she had not said. The red scarf was the sort of small fact that might have changed everything three years ago, and yet it was Daniel's secret, given in trust in a quiet room. She decided to wait a little longer, and she hated herself a little for waiting, although she could not have said which duty she was failing.

Pell fed the pages of the diary through a copying machine in the corridor, and handed Marianne a set, because she wanted to know what a counselor made of them. At the same time she warned her, firmly and kindly, not to play detective, because that was exactly how people got hurt. Marianne promised, and she meant it, at least at the moment of promising, although she was already thinking of a red door on Harbour Row.

Out on the steps of the police station the noon sun was bright, and the harbour glittered at the end of the street. Marianne put the copies in her bag and looked again at the first page of the diary, where Anna had written her address, Number Four, Harbour Row. She had never met the landlady, but she decided that she would go there now, before she could think better of it.

Number Four, Harbour Row, was a small terraced house with a glossy red door and a brass knocker polished to a shine. The door opened at the very first knock, and a tiny, white-haired woman in a flowered apron looked Marianne up and down with eyes as sharp as a bird's. She said nothing at all, and Marianne had the distinct impression of being weighed.

Mrs Dunn announced that she knew perfectly well who Marianne was, since Daniel Reeve had once mentioned her, quite kindly, while mending the clock on her mantelpiece. Without waiting for a reply she led her through to a kitchen crowded with knitting and plants, and put the kettle on the stove. It was clear that the old lady had long been waiting for somebody to come and ask her questions.

When the tea was poured, Mrs Dunn took her up a steep little staircase to a narrow room with a bare shelf, a made bed and a window that looked out over the roofs to the harbour. She had not had the heart to let it to anyone since Anna died, she confessed, though her pension would have been the better for the rent. The room smelled faintly of lavender and of dust, and it seemed to Marianne that the air in it had not been moved for three years.

Anna had been the neatest lodger she ever had, Mrs Dunn said, always humming on the stairs and always leaving the bathroom cleaner than she found it. In her last few weeks, however, the humming had stopped, and the girl had begun to leave her dinner half eaten and to walk the quay late at night. A person who loves a girl notices such things, she added, even if she says nothing.

One evening, as they washed up together, Anna had told her that on Friday she had to speak to someone and that she was dreading it. Mrs Dunn had asked who, and Anna had only shaken her head and smiled in a way that was not really a smile. It was the last proper conversation that the two of them ever had, and the old lady had turned it over in her mind a thousand times since.

On that Friday evening Anna had come downstairs at eight o'clock and wrapped her long red scarf twice around her neck, the one that her brother had given her. Mrs Dunn remembered it perfectly, she said, and she remembered, too, that in three years no officer of the law had ever thought to ask her what the girl was wearing. Marianne felt her heart beat a little faster, for here was a witness to the scarf that nobody had ever troubled to question.

On the windowsill stood a vase of dried flowers, brown and brittle with age, and Mrs Dunn said that they had been brought by Owen Marsh. After the funeral he had come to the house with fresh flowers every month for a whole year, sitting in the kitchen with his hat on his knees, and she had thought him a very kind man. She was no longer quite so sure of that, and she had begun to wonder what the kindness had been meant to buy.

A week after the funeral, however, he had asked her, very casually, whether Anna had left any papers from the shop in her room, any books or letters or notes. Mrs Dunn had told him that there was nothing, except that she had seen Anna post a parcel to her brother on the Thursday, the day before she died. He had thanked her, and he had gone on thanking her, for rather longer than the answer deserved.

Mrs Dunn peered at Marianne over the top of her glasses and said that kind men can have reasons for their kindness, and that she was an old woman who had known a few. She had not liked the way he asked about the papers, she said, nor the way he had stood afterwards in her hall, looking at the stairs. She had told no one, because no one had asked, and because she had no proof of anything.

At the door she pressed a framed photograph into Marianne's hands, a young woman in a red scarf, laughing on the quay with her hair blown across her face. Marianne thanked her, and promised to bring it back, and walked away down Harbour Row with the picture held against her chest. In her mind there was a single name that she did not like, and she could no longer pretend that it was not there.

Marianne walked down to the harbour, where the fishing boats rocked against the old stone wall and the gulls shrieked and wheeled overhead. The air smelled of salt, tar and fish, and the tide slapped and sucked among the pilings as though it were whispering to itself. She was looking for the Fish Steps, because she wanted to stand where Anna had last stood.

She found them at the far end of the quay, a narrow flight of ancient steps that descended between two rusty rails into the dark water. Thick green weed clung to the lower stones, and with the tide so high there was barely a handbreadth of dry step left above the waves. It was easy to see how a foot might slip there, even on a calm night.

Marianne stood at the top with one hand on the cold iron rail and tried to imagine the scene as Daniel had told it to her. A frightened young woman, with the wind behind her voice, had stood here at nine o'clock on a Friday evening and telephoned her brother, saying that she had found something wrong. She had not known that she was speaking to him for the last time.

A harsh voice shattered her thoughts, and a big man in a heavy coat came striding along the quay with his fists clenched and his face dark red. He was, she would learn, Gareth Pike, the harbour master, and he shouted at her to get away from the steps and leave his harbour alone. A pair of gulls rose screaming from the wall, as if they too had been rebuked.

Marianne turned to face him, keeping her hands open and her shoulders low, and gave her name in the calm, unhurried voice that had steadied a thousand frightened people. She asked him politely for his own, and the big man, who had been braced for an argument, stopped short a few paces off. He seemed to have no plan at all for what should come after the shouting, and he stood there with his mouth a little open.

As he glared at her, she noticed behind him a blue tarpaulin tied carefully over some shapes beside the harbour office, with the corner of a rusty drum showing beneath. It was a fuel store, and a small hand pump stood next to it, and no sign anywhere declared who owned them. Pike saw where her eyes had gone, and his face changed from red to the colour of old candle wax.

The anger drained out of him all at once, and he looked, for a moment, merely afraid, like a boy who has been caught with something in his pocket. He took her for an inspector or a policewoman in plain clothes, and she told him that she was neither, and that she had no intention of reporting what she had seen. She said it so gently, and with so little sign of triumph, that he believed her at once and almost wished that he did not.

Pike leaned heavily on a drum with his hands deep in his coat pockets, and gruffly admitted that he had been selling fuel from it for years, cheap and without paying the tax. On the night that the girl died he had been selling it too, he said, and that was the reason he had never offered a word to anyone. He did not look at Marianne once while he spoke, but kept his eyes fixed on the grey water beyond the wall.

Then, slowly, as though the words were being pulled out of him, he raised one thick finger and pointed along the quay toward the head of the steps. At about nine o'clock that night, he said, he had looked up from his work and seen a young woman in a bright red scarf, talking quietly with a man in a long dark coat. They had stood very close together, he added, like people who know each other.

He had not seen the man's face, and he had not stayed to watch, for he had been more afraid of his own secret than curious about theirs. He had gone back into his office and shut the door, and in the morning he had heard that a girl had been found in the harbour. He had never spoken of it from that day to this, and the silence had sat in him like a stone.

Dusk had fallen when Marianne heard a quick, anxious knock at her cottage door, and she opened it to find Tilly Ames on the step, breathless and pink. The girl had not been able to stop thinking about Daniel all day, she explained, and she had remembered something that she had not thought important. She held a thick book against her chest like a shield, and it was plain that she had run most of the way.

Tilly laid her fat appointment book on the kitchen table and turned the pages back through the year, running her finger down the entries for Daniel Reeve. Beside his name, week after week, she had written the same small note, that Mr Marsh had telephoned on the Thursday to confirm the hour of the Friday visit. He had never missed a single week in all those months, and Tilly had thought it merely the habit of a careful man.

She pointed next to the column of bills, where a second, smaller note recurred again and again in her round handwriting. Mr Marsh had always paid Daniel's fees in cash, she said, handing the notes over at the desk with a smile and insisting that he was only helping a friend. At the time it had seemed to her the most generous thing in the world.

Marianne stared at the page while the cat slept beside the stove, and a thought that she did not like began to take shape in her mind. A man who knew every appointment and paid every fee might also have wished to know, as exactly as possible, how much his friend was telling the woman who listened to him. She had been, she realised, a kind of window, and someone had been looking through it.

Marianne telephoned Pell, who said grudgingly that they might look at Daniel's flat, provided a constable went with them and nothing was moved. Soon the two women were walking through the lamplit streets toward Water Lane, Tilly clutching Marianne's sleeve in the dark. The wind had risen again, and somewhere out over the harbour a bell was ringing on a buoy.

Constable Abel Frost, a young man with a steady manner and a large torch, was waiting at the door of the flat, and he told them that they had ten minutes. He asked them to touch nothing, and to tell him at once if anything looked wrong, and he followed a pace behind them like a polite shadow. The door closed behind the three of them with a soft click, and the silence of the empty flat settled over them.

The rooms were bare and scrupulously tidy: one chair, one cup upside down on the draining board, and a long wall of clocks, every one of them silent. Each had stopped at a quarter past nine, exactly like the clocks in the shop, so that the flat seemed to be waiting inside a single frozen moment. Marianne felt her throat tighten, for she knew how many Fridays this man had spent here alone.

By the window stood a workbench with a lamp, a loupe and a half-built silver watch, its delicate wheels still lying open to the air. Beside it, in a plain wooden frame, was a photograph of Anna, laughing, with her head thrown back. Tilly whispered that he must have been making it for her birthday, and that he had never been able to finish it.

On the kitchen table lay a paper calendar, and the Friday that had just passed was circled in thick pencil, as though it had been marked for weeks. In the margin beside it, in his small upright hand, Daniel had written the words Tell M C, and then underlined them twice. Marianne read them and felt, absurdly, that she had been given an order and a compliment at once.

Beside the front door a row of small brass hooks held labelled keys, for the shop, the workshop, the cellar and the cupboard, and one hook, marked Tower, was empty. Marianne noticed it, and the little brass label stayed in her mind even as the constable ushered them out into the windy dark. She thought nothing of it then, and she would think of little else later.

On Sunday morning the church bells rolled out across the roofs of Saltmere, one after another, and Biscuit stretched himself luxuriously on the bed as if nothing in the world were wrong. Marianne lay still and listened, having hardly slept, and went through the day's possibilities in her mind. There was still no news of Daniel, and every hour that passed made the silence more serious.

A message from Pell was waiting on her telephone, brief and tired, and spoken in the flat voice of a person who has been up half the night. She was on her way to Carrow, she said, to see the watch dealer whose card had been in the envelope, and she would not be back in Saltmere before evening. She asked Marianne, once more and quite politely, to leave the investigating to the police and to stay out of harm's way.

Marianne found that she could not bear to sit at home with the cat and her thoughts, so she put a roll of tape in her pocket and went down to the office. She climbed the stairs past the warm smell of the bakery, past the shuttered desk where Tilly used to sit, and into the room where she had spent half her life. She had not finished packing, and her hands badly needed something to do, since her mind would not leave her alone.

After a while she lowered herself into Daniel's chair and looked slowly round the room as he must have seen it, week after week, from that one fixed point. There was the bare shelf, the two empty cups, the box of tissues and the long window beyond them, and in the window, filling the whole of the glass, stood the Harbour Clock Tower. For eight months it had been almost the only thing that he had looked at, and she wondered what he had seen in it.

She took Anna's diary pages from her bag, spread them across the desk, and read them through again from the first line to the last. This time the single letter O seemed to leap out from the text, the way a face can leap from a crowd once one knows whom to look for. She read the passage three times, and still the letter would not turn into anything else.

On a clean sheet of paper she wrote the name of every person whom Anna had mentioned, or could have known, in connection with the shop. One by one she crossed them out, the tradesmen, the customers, the neighbours and the council clerk, until only a single name remained. It began with O, and it belonged to a man who had shaken her hand with both of his own.

Marianne rubbed her eyes and leaned back among the packing cases, telling herself sternly that she had no proof whatever. Owen Marsh had done nothing but be kind, paying a friend's bills, bringing flowers to a grave, and hurrying into a shop when he heard that something was wrong. The whole thing might be an old woman's gossip and a young woman's pencil marks, and a counselor above all people ought to hold her conclusions loosely.

Then, quite suddenly, she remembered what Daniel had said to her only two days earlier, that there had been one person he trusted above all others. He had never named that person, and it came to her with a small cold shock why a man might find it impossible to say aloud the name of his only friend. The silence of eight months had not been emptiness, she saw, but a strange and painful kind of loyalty that she had mistaken for coldness.

The afternoon wore on, and the light in the window turned slowly to gold, and the clock tower threw a long shadow across the harbour. At about four o'clock she heard footsteps on the stair, light and quick and unhurried, and then two soft knocks on the half-open door. She looked up, with the diary pages still spread in front of her, and felt her heart stop for the space of a breath.

Owen Marsh stood in the doorway in his fine long coat, carrying a small tray with two paper cups of steaming coffee, and wearing the most pleasant of smiles. He said that he had seen her light and thought that she would need something hot after such a long and worrying weekend. She slid the diary pages into the drawer of the desk before she answered, and asked him in.

Owen set the tray down among the packing boxes and took the chair opposite hers, the same chair in which Daniel had sat for eight months. He talked warmly about his friend, in the low, anxious tones of a man who had not slept, and about how helpless it felt to watch a person drift further away each year. Marianne listened, nodded, and said very little, waiting with her cup in both hands to see what he had really come for.

He glanced around at the bare shelves and the stacked boxes and asked whether she was truly leaving, as though the idea distressed him. Daniel owed her a great deal, he said, more than he knew, and it seemed hard that her last week should be spoiled by such a business. His sympathy flowed easily, and she noted, with a growing coldness that she hid behind her cup, how very smoothly it flowed.

He told her that Inspector Pell had called at the shop that morning, asking more questions about the two cups, and he leaned back and stared down into his coffee as though the answers might be waiting at the bottom. A small silence fell, and in it she heard the faint rattle of a baker's tray on the floor below, and Owen cleared his throat. He went on, as though he had decided something, in the same easy and sorrowful voice as before.

He began to talk about Anna, with deep and apparently genuine sorrow, saying that it was he who had first brought her to the shop and given her the books to keep. She had been cheerful and quick and clever, he said, and she had made the accounts look like a pleasure, and he still could not believe that she was gone. He spoke slowly, like a man picking his way over stones in the dark, and he never once looked her in the eye.

Then he rubbed his forehead with the heel of his hand and confessed, in a low and unguarded voice, that he still dreamed about her, even now, three years afterwards. In the dream, he said, he always saw her red scarf lying on the harbour steps, bright against the wet grey stone, and he could never reach it before he woke. The words seemed to leave his mouth before he had decided to say them.

Marianne's cup stopped halfway to her lips, and for a moment the whole room seemed to tilt. The scarf had never been found, not on the steps, not on the quay, not in the water, so there was no reason in the world why anyone should picture it lying anywhere at all. A man does not dream so exactly of a thing that he has never seen.

She set down her cup, reached for no pen, and wrote nothing, but kept on her face the gentle, ordinary expression that she had worn for thirty years across a thousand desks. Inside, her mind was racing, laying one fact upon another, and the pieces of the puzzle seemed to fall into place with small, dreadful clicks. She sipped her coffee, which tasted of nothing at all, and waited for him to say more.

Owen leaned forward with a gentle smile and asked, as if it hardly mattered, whether Daniel had ever said anything about him in their sessions. His voice was easy, but his eyes were fixed on her face and were not smiling at all. In the stillness she could hear her own pulse, and she hoped that he could not.

Marianne met his gaze quite steadily and shook her head, slowly, with a regretful air that she did not feel. She said, with perfect courtesy, that she could never repeat what a client told her, not to a friend, not to a stranger, not to anyone, and that this had been the first rule of her working life. His smile did not vanish, but it grew very thin, like ice on a pond in the first hour of the thaw.

Owen rose, brushed down his fine coat, and said lightly that he would let her get on with her packing, and that she must tell him first, before anyone, if Daniel got in touch. At the door he turned and gave her one last long look, and then he was gone, and his footsteps faded away down the stair. Marianne sat quite still, as though she had been holding her breath for an hour.

Marianne waited, quite motionless, until she heard the bakery bell jangle below and the street door close, and only then did she allow herself to breathe. Her hands began to shake so violently that she had to clasp them together in her lap, like a child at a funeral. For a long moment she could do nothing but listen to the thudding of her own heart.

She took Daniel's folder from the drawer and opened it at the notes for the third session, though she knew perfectly well what they said. There it was in her own small pencil, with the double underline: Anna's red scarf never found, told no one else. The page was dry and ordinary, and it was suddenly the most important page in the building.

She picked up the telephone and rang Pell's number, but the call went to a recorded voice asking her to leave a message after the tone. Pell was somewhere in Carrow, in a workshop or on a train, and perhaps her telephone was switched off, as telephones so often are in the moments that matter most. Marianne waited for the tone, and drew a deep breath, knowing that whatever she said next could never be unsaid.

She spoke slowly and clearly, giving the facts in order: the scarf that had never been found, what Daniel had said in the third session, and the words Owen had let fall over his coffee. In doing so she broke the promise that she had kept for thirty years, and was astonished to find that it felt less like a betrayal than like opening a window. She ended the message with her name, the time and the number of her telephone, and then she sat quite still, amazed at herself.

Then she telephoned Tilly and asked, as lightly as she could, whether there was any place in Saltmere to which Owen Marsh might take a person, any place for which he held the keys. Tilly thought for a moment and said that Marsh and Reeve looked after the Harbour Clock Tower for the town council, and that both partners had keys to the door and the stair. Marianne thanked her, said that it was nothing, and rang off before the girl could ask her anything else.

She crossed to the window, without quite knowing why, and looked out across the rooftops at the great stone tower on the quay, which she had watched so often that she hardly saw it any more. The late sun lay along its grey flank, and the white dial shone like a coin. She stood very still, because something about it was wrong, and she could not at first say what.

It was the hands of the clock, she realised after a moment, which were quite plainly in the wrong place. They stood together at a quarter past nine, in the golden light of an afternoon that was nearly over, and the minute hand did not so much as tremble. A clock that had kept the town's time for a hundred years does not show the wrong hour for no reason, and a quarter past nine was the one hour that she could not mistake.

That very morning, on her way down Quay Street, she had glanced up at the dial, and it had told the right time, so somebody must have stopped it, and set its hands, within the last few hours. She gripped the window frame until her knuckles whitened, and the stone of the tower seemed to swim before her eyes. A tower clock does not stop itself, and it does not forget to strike the hour.

She thought of the little silver watch on the table, and of the silent clocks in the shop and in the flat, every one halted at the same minute, and the pieces fell into place with a click. It was not grief that had stopped this clock, nor chance, but a human hand, and the hand had wished to be understood. It was a message, and it was addressed, she was quite certain, to the one person who had seen the watch and knew what it meant.

Only two men in Saltmere could climb that stair and reach that mechanism, and one of them had just walked out of her office with a smile. The other had left the hook for his own tower key empty beside his front door, and had since vanished from the face of the earth. Daniel, she knew with perfect certainty, was in the tower, and he was alive enough to ask for help.

She rang Pell's number once more, and then the police station, where a tired desk officer told her that the inspector was still out of town and that Constable Frost would not be on duty until six. He promised, with the weary courtesy of a man who has heard too many anxious callers, to pass on her message as soon as he was able. It was not nearly good enough, and she knew it as she put the receiver down, with the sun already sinking toward the roofs.

She took a torch from the drawer of her desk and put it into one coat pocket, and into the other she slipped the little knife that she used to cut tape, feeling faintly ridiculous as she did so. Every instinct of her profession told her to wait, to listen, and to let the proper authorities act, but she could hear the minutes running away like water from a tap. There was nobody else who would go, and nobody else who knew what she knew.

She went down the stairs past the bakery, where the last loaves of the day were cooling on their racks, and out into a wind that smelled of rain and weed. The boats along the quay creaked at their moorings, a chain rattled somewhere, and the light had begun to take on the grey-gold tone that comes before the dusk. She walked quickly, with her collar turned up and her eyes on the tower.

Gareth Pike was standing at the door of the harbour office with a mug of tea, and to her surprise he greeted her quite politely, even with a trace of embarrassment, as one greets a person who has been kind. She asked him whether he had seen anything unusual near the clock tower during the past two days, and he frowned and set down his mug. He took a long time to answer, scratching his chin, as though he were afraid of what the answer might mean.

On Friday evening, just after six, he said slowly, he had seen Owen Marsh half walking and half carrying a stumbling man toward the tower, and he had taken the stranger for drunk. He remembered the long dark coat that Owen wore, and as he said it his big face turned the colour of putty. It was the coat, he whispered, that he had seen on the steps three years ago.

Pike snatched up the telephone on his desk and said that he would call the police at once, and the harbour constable too, and come after her as fast as his legs could carry him. Marianne told him firmly to wait at the foot of the tower for them and not to climb alone, for there was no sense in two of them walking into a room where they did not know what waited. He nodded, but she was not at all sure that he had heard a single word of what she had said.

He held up a thick finger as she turned to go, and warned her that the stair had a hundred and twelve steps, no light, and a loose rail near the top. She said that she would remember, and she thanked him, and was surprised to find that she meant it. He watched her go with an odd, humble look on his big face, like a man who has just been given a second chance.

She walked on along the harbour wall as the last light drained out of the sky, and behind her the lamps of the quay came on, one by one, each in its own small circle of yellow. The sea had turned the colour of slate, and the tower ahead grew taller and darker with every step. She did not allow herself to look back, because she knew that if she did she might lose her nerve altogether.

At the head of the Fish Steps she stopped for a moment, with one hand on the cold rail and her breath coming short, and looked down at the black water slapping against the weed. She thought of Anna, who had stood on this very spot three years before, and of the man who had stood with her, and she felt something close to anger. Then she drew a long breath, tightened her grip on the torch, and walked on toward the tower without looking down again.

At last the Harbour Clock Tower rose in front of her, square and tall against a sky the colour of a bruise, its white dial shining faintly with the two hands stopped at a quarter past nine. At its foot stood a small wooden door, studded with iron nails, and it was standing slightly open. Someone, she thought, had not wanted to be heard unlocking it, or had forgotten to lock it again.

Marianne pushed the little door wide and stepped into the dark foot of the tower, where the wind fell away at once and a deep, cold quiet closed round her. The air smelled of old stone, of machine oil and of something older still, like the inside of a well. She stood for a moment in the blackness with her heart knocking against her ribs, listening to the silence of a place that did not want to be disturbed.

She switched on her torch and its thin beam climbed a spiral of worn stone steps, each one hollowed in the middle by the feet of generations of clockmakers. Holding the iron rail with one hand and the torch in the other, she began to climb, trying to make her footsteps as light as a cat's. The stair turned, and turned again, and the small door far below was lost in the darkness, so that she felt there was no way back except to go on.

At every turn there was a narrow slit in the wall, hardly wider than a hand, and through each one she saw a little more of the town spread out below her. The harbour lamps looked small and far away, like the lights of a toy village, and the sea beyond them had melted into the night. She wondered whether Daniel had ever looked out through those slits, on long nights when the tower clock needed his care, and thought of Anna.

She counted the steps to keep her mind steady, as she had once counted breaths with frightened clients, and at fifty she was obliged to stop and rest with her hand flat against the cold wall. She was sixty-two years old, and her knees reminded her of it with every turn. Yet she did not for one moment consider turning back, because the thought of Daniel, alone in the dark above her, was stronger than any weariness.

On a landing she passed a faded council notice, curling at the corners, which announced the hours when the tower was open to visitors, and beside it a cracked old clock dial leaning against the wall. Dust lay thick on everything except the steps, which had lately been scuffed by hurrying feet. Marianne bent and touched the stone with her fingertips, and found it marked with the prints of boots.

She was climbing again when she heard a faint sound somewhere above her, a dull, slow tapping, like metal knocking against stone. She stopped and held her breath, and for a moment she could hear nothing but the blood in her ears and the far cry of a gull. Then it came again, quite clearly, from high up in the dark, a dull knock and a pause and then another knock, as steady as the beat of a heart.

She stood quite still and listened, and the tapping went on, patient and regular, with a gap between each stroke as long as a breath. It was not the sound of a machine, for every clock in the tower had been silenced, and it was not the sound of a rat or the wind. It was the sound of a person, trying to be heard, and she began to climb faster.

Higher up the stair grew narrower and steeper, and she passed beneath the great bronze bell, which hung in the darkness above her head like the shadow of a sleeping animal. A single breath of air from a window moved the rope that hung beside it, and the rope stirred and was still. She kept her torch low and her breath quiet, and she did not touch anything.

At last, at the top of a final steep flight, she saw a thin line of yellow lamplight under a heavy wooden door, the only light in the whole of the tower. The tapping was coming from behind it, quite distinct now, and she realised that it was keeping time with her own pulse. She turned off her torch and stood in the dark for a moment, listening to the tapping and to the quiet roaring of her own blood.

She put her hand on the cold iron latch and felt it tremble under her fingers, though she could not tell whether the tremor was in the metal or in her own hand. In thirty years she had opened a great many doors for frightened people, and never once had she been so afraid of what lay behind one. She drew in a long breath, said a silent word to whatever watches over frightened people, and pushed the heavy door open with her shoulder.

The clock room was a high stone chamber crowded with great iron wheels, rods and chains, all of them dark with oil and age, and not one of them moved. The silence was so deep that Marianne could hear the whisper of her own breathing and the faint ringing in her ears. It was like stepping into the sleeping heart of some enormous animal, and every shadow seemed to hold its breath along with her.

In the middle of the room hung the great pendulum on its iron rod, perfectly still, like a pause in the middle of a sentence. A single oil lamp burned on the floor, throwing monstrous shadows of wheels and levers across the walls, and the cold air smelled of paraffin and rust. She stood for a long moment, afraid to move and afraid to stay, while her eyes slowly learned to read the shapes in the dark.

Beside the pendulum, in the yellow circle of the lamplight, sat a thin man tied to a wooden chair with a coil of thick cord, his head bowed on his chest. She knew the oil-stained hands and the narrow shoulders before she saw his face, and her breath left her in a rush. It was Daniel, and he was alive, and for a moment nothing else in the world mattered to her at all, not the stair, nor Owen, nor the fear.

Marianne crossed the floor in three strides and knelt in front of him, saying his name softly and then again, more urgently. He lifted his head slowly, as if it were very heavy, and his dry lips shaped her own name without making much sound. His eyes were clouded with weariness and with whatever drug had been put into his tea, but they knew her, and that was enough.

A plastic bottle of water stood on the stone floor beside the chair, half empty and out of his reach. She unscrewed it, held it carefully to his mouth, and tipped it a little at a time, and he drank like a man who had not tasted water for days. When he had finished he let out a long, shuddering breath, and a little colour came back into his grey face like the first light of morning.

In a hoarse whisper, Daniel told her that on Friday, after he left her office, he had gone back to the shop to speak to Owen, and that Owen had made him a cup of tea. It had tasted bitter, he said, and he remembered nothing after that, until he woke in the dark with his wrists burning. He did not say that he had been foolish, but she saw him think it.

Since then Owen had climbed the stair twice a day, bringing water, a little bread, and always the same question, which he put in the gentlest possible voice. He wanted to know where Anna's account book was, and what Daniel had done with it, and who else had seen it. Daniel had told him nothing at all, and he had been quietly proud of that, in the way that a man is proud of a small thing in a very great trouble.

He smiled faintly, with cracked lips, and nodded toward the pendulum that hung beside them, so close that his fingers could almost touch the rod. Slowly, through the long afternoon, he explained, he had worked his right hand free of the cord and reached the small brass wheel that moved the hands. He had turned them to a quarter past nine, and then caught the pendulum and held it still, hoping, he whispered, that somebody who had seen his watch would understand.

Marianne took out her little knife, the one she had used for packing tape, and began to saw at the thick cord around his wrists. The knots were tight and the cord was hard and wet with sweat, and her cold fingers slipped again and again on the handle. She worked as fast as she dared, murmuring to him all the while, and each strand parted with a small, reluctant sigh.

She had loosened barely half of it when she heard a sound from the stair below them, faint at first and then unmistakable. It was the noise of boots on stone, mounting steadily, with the slow, unhurried rhythm of a man who knew every step and had no reason to fear what lay at the top. Daniel's face turned the colour of paper, and in the lamplight she saw him close his eyes, as a man does who has been waiting a long time for a blow.

Marianne's hands froze on the cord, and Daniel's eyes opened wide and met hers across the lamplight. He whispered, so faintly that she barely heard it, that she must hide behind the wheels while there was still time, and that she must not try to help him. She shook her head, once, and went on holding his gaze, for she had never in her life walked away from a person who was afraid.

She knew that she could not leave him, and she knew too that she could not fight a man of Owen's size with a little knife and sixty-two years of experience. She folded the blade, slid it into her pocket, and stood up in front of the chair with her hands open and empty at her sides. If there was to be a battle, it would be fought with the only weapons she had ever trusted.

The door swung inward, and Owen walked into the lamplight with a torch in one hand and a paper bag in the other, the smell of hot bread and fried onions coming off it. He stopped dead on the threshold, and the bag slipped a little in his fingers, so that for an instant he looked quite ridiculous. It was an ordinary supper, carried up an ordinary stair, and it made the whole scene more terrible.

For a long moment nobody spoke or moved, and the flame of the oil lamp leaned over in a draught from the stair. Then the warm, friendly look fell away from Owen's face like a mask, and what lay beneath it was tired, grey and old. It was the face, Marianne thought, of a man who has long since stopped believing in his own cheerfulness.

Owen stepped into the doorway and filled it with his coat and his shoulders, so that there was no way out except past him. He said, in a quiet, almost conversational tone, that Marianne had listened too well, and that he had known it from the very first time he heard her name. There was no anger in his voice, which was the worst thing about it.

He told her that he ought never to have paid for Daniel's sessions, nor stayed so close to her office, nor come to drink her coffee, and that each mistake had felt like cleverness at the time. His voice was flat and level, like that of a man reading a list of his own errors in a language he no longer understood. He did not seem to expect an answer, and he did not seem to care very much whether she heard him or not.

Marianne rose slowly from her knees and spoke in the steady, quiet voice that she had used on frightened people for thirty years. She did not ask him about Daniel, or about the cord, or about the paper bag, but about Owen himself, and she asked what had been happening to him. It was the one question that nobody had put to him in years, and she saw it land like a stone in still water.

Owen gave a short, bitter laugh that went echoing away among the iron wheels, and for a moment his whole body shook with it. Nobody had asked him that, he said, not once, in three years, not even himself, and the sound of the question seemed to take him by surprise. He stared at her as if she had spoken in a foreign language, and then, very slowly, he began to look like a man who wanted to answer.

Marianne folded her hands in front of her and said that she had all night, and that there was no one to hurry them. She asked him, very gently, to sit down and tell her, and she did not look at the door or at the torch in his hand. She had learned long ago that the quietest voice is the one that is heard.

Owen looked at her for a long time, as if weighing something that could not be weighed, and then, slowly, his shoulders dropped. He sat down heavily on the stone step beside the door, and set his torch between his boots with the beam pointing at the floor. He looked, in that moment, like an exhausted child who has been up far past his bedtime.

Owen stared at the floor between his boots and began to talk, in a low, even voice, like a man who has rehearsed a speech so many times that it has worn smooth. The shop, he said, had been losing money for years, and he had been too proud to say so to Daniel, who never looked at the figures and trusted him completely. It had seemed, at first, a small problem with a simple answer, the kind that a clever man could solve before anyone noticed.

He had started by selling an old watch or two, ones that customers had left for repair and never come back to claim, sitting forgotten in a drawer at the back of the workroom. Nobody had missed them, and the money had paid the rent for a month, and so he had sold another, and then another. Daniel never checked the shelves, because he had never in his life imagined that he needed to.

He had inscribed the initials D and R in the ledger, he said, so that the transactions would pass for Daniel's work, and he had promised himself that he would restore every penny the moment the business recovered. It was merely a loan, he had whispered to himself at night, extracted from strangers who would never notice the loss. He repeated the excuse now as if he were hearing, for the first time, how little it weighed.

Anna, he said, was the one person clever enough to see it, and she saw it as a good bookkeeper would, from the pattern of the columns rather than from any single page. She did not shout or threaten him, but came to him kindly, the way one visits a friend who is ill, and told him that she wanted to hear his side before she said a word to anyone. He could still hear her voice, he said, kind and level and patient, and it was that kindness which he found hardest to bear.

She asked him to meet her on the Friday night, away from the shop and the customers and the telephone, and he suggested the harbour, because it was quiet. They agreed on the Fish Steps, where nobody would see them after dark, and where she liked to sit and think with her feet above the water. He had gone, he said, believing that he could talk her round, as he had talked round a great many people in his life, and he had worn his best coat.

On the steps she had told him, in a quiet voice that had no cruelty in it at all, that he must tell Daniel the truth by Monday morning. If he did not, she said, she would have to tell Daniel herself, and she would help him to explain it, and she would stand beside him when he did. It was a generous offer, and he had never forgiven her for it, because it left him no one but himself to blame.

Owen said that he had begged her to wait, and that she had shaken her head, kindly but firmly, and turned to go up the steps. Then her foot had slid on the green weed, and with one short cry, almost without surprise, she had gone down into the black water of the harbour. It had happened so quickly that there had not seemed to be any time between the one moment and the other.

He had reached out and tried to catch her, and her long red scarf had come away in his hand, as light as nothing, and then she was in the water and the tide was high. He could not swim well, he said, and he was so afraid, so completely and shamefully afraid, that instead of shouting for help he had turned and run. He had told himself that someone else would hear her, and that a better man would surely reach her first, and then he had stopped telling himself anything.

He had dropped the scarf on the steps without knowing that he had done it, and he had run all the way home, and he had never gone back. In his sleep ever since he had seen it lying there on the wet stone, bright as a flag, while the water rose and rose toward it. He had never told a living soul, he said, and he was astonished to hear it now, in his own voice, in this cold stone room.

Marianne knelt on the stone floor within an arm's length of him, with her hand open and still on her knee, as she had knelt beside a hundred other people at the edge of an unbearable truth. She told him quietly that he had carried this secret alone for three years, and that nobody can carry such a weight for ever. He could put it down now, she said, and she would stay with him while he did.

Owen's shoulders began to shake, and he said hoarsely that if he let them walk out of that room he would lose everything, his shop, his name and his freedom. Marianne answered, with great gentleness, that he had already lost it all on the night of the harbour steps, and that only the truth was left for him to keep. He put his hands over his face, and for a while the only sound in the room was the sound of a grown man weeping.

Far below them, faint but unmistakable, came the sound of voices and the heavy ring of boots mounting the stone steps, and then a woman's voice shouting upward, sharp and clear, with a note of real fear in it. It was Inspector Pell, and she was calling Marianne's name over and over again. The sound echoed around the tower like the tolling of a different, human bell.

Owen raised his head and looked at the door, and then at the torch between his boots, and Marianne watched the last of the struggle go out of his face. He set the torch down on the stone floor, slowly and carefully, as a man might lay down a heavy burden, and lifted his empty hands to the level of his shoulders. Then he sat quite still on the cold flagstones, waiting for whatever was to come.

The door crashed open and Inspector Pell burst into the clock room, with Constable Frost close behind her and a second torch cutting a bright path through the shadows. She took in the whole scene in a single glance, the lamp, the chair, the cords and the man on the floor, and her face hardened and then, very slightly, relaxed. In a calm, formal voice she arrested Owen Marsh, and he did not resist.

Constable Frost drew a clasp knife from his belt, knelt behind the chair, and cut the last of the cords that bound Daniel's wrists and ankles, which slid away across the stone. Daniel sat for a moment, rubbing his arms and breathing carefully, as if he had forgotten that he could move at all. Then the constable took him gently under the elbow, and helped him to his feet.

Daniel stood unsteadily in the cold clock room, close enough to Marianne that she could feel the faint warmth of him, and for a moment neither of them said anything at all. Then he looked at her, with his clouded eyes quite clear, and said quietly, “You came,” and she answered, “Of course”. It was the plainest conversation she had ever had, and she knew that she would remember it for the rest of her life.

Pell explained, with her hand on the back of the iron chair, that Marianne's message had reached her on the train home from Carrow, where the watch dealer had picked out Owen's photograph at once. Gareth Pike had telephoned the station while she was still on the road, she said, babbling something about a coat and a staircase, and between the two of them they had quite enough to act on. She had driven faster than she cared to admit, she said, and she had never in her life been so glad to reach a staircase.

Daniel crossed the floor with slow, careful steps to the great mechanism, and laid one hand upon a long iron lever, as a rider lays his hand on the neck of a horse. The pendulum shuddered, swung, and began to move, the wheels turned in their order, and a moment later the great bell above them struck, a deep bronze note that rolled out across the sleeping town. He had set the hands to the true time, and outside they began, once more, to creep forward from that dreadful minute.

Gareth Pike appeared at the head of the stairs, grey in the face and gasping for breath, with a lantern in his hand and an expression of terrible resolve. He said, before anyone could speak to him, that he had something to tell the inspector, and that he had waited three years too long to say it. On the morning after Anna died he had found her red scarf lying on the harbour steps, and in his fear of questions about his fuel he had thrown it into his stove.

Marianne went down the long stair on Pell's arm, one slow step at a time, with Daniel walking ahead of them on the constable's arm and the lantern throwing their shadows huge on the curving wall. At the bottom the cold night air met her like water on a hot face, and she saw that the lamps of the harbour were all shining as usual. Somewhere above them, steady and clear, the tower clock was ticking again, and she thought that it had never sounded so sweet.

On Monday morning Marianne gave her statement at a table in a bright, busy room of the police station, with a mug of tea going cold at her elbow and a young officer typing as she spoke. When she had finished, Inspector Pell read it through slowly from start to finish, signed it, and told her that she had been right to break her silence. Daniel, she added, might well not have been found in time if she had kept it.

Pell laid on her desk a laboratory report, a page of the false sales from the ledger, and a receipt book that Mr Lunt had sent by the first train. The cup from the workbench had held a strong sleeping drug, and none of the forged signatures bore the tiny clock hand that Daniel put to everything he made. It was, she said, the sort of mistake that a careless liar makes, by forgetting that other people look at the details.

Owen had meant to keep Daniel in the tower until he found where the ledger was hidden, Pell explained, and then to let the town believe that the clockmaker was a thief who had run away. He had sworn, in his own way, that no one should be hurt, and he had gone on swearing it even as he turned the key. Gareth Pike would answer for his fuel, she added, but his evidence would count in his favour.

On Tuesday afternoon the autumn sun lay in long bars across two chairs in an empty office above the bakery, where the shelves were bare and the boxes had gone. Daniel Reeve arrived at four exactly, as he always had, thinner and paler than before but quite steady on his feet. This time he had not come to be silent, and she saw it in his face before he spoke, and her own heart lifted.

He sat down in his usual chair, took the little silver watch from his pocket, and set it upon the table between them, as he had done on the day that all this began. For a long while he looked at it, and then he asked, very simply, how a person began, when there was so much to say. Marianne smiled, and told him that anywhere would do, that there was no right place to start and no hurry at all.

So Daniel began, and for an hour he talked about Anna, about their childhood by the sea, her terrible singing and her wonderful sums, and the long, empty years since her last phone call. Marianne said very little, as she had always done, but now her silence was a doorway and not a wall. The light moved slowly across the floor, and neither of them looked at the clock.

When he had finished there were tears on his cheeks, but his shoulders had come down from around his ears, and he looked, she thought, ten years younger. Marianne took the brass key from her pocket, the one that he had pressed into her hand on the last Friday, and laid it in his open palm. It was his to keep, she said, or to throw into the sea, whichever he found easier to carry on the days to come.

She walked him to the door and watched him go down the stairs, and then she went back and stood for a minute in the empty room, which smelled of dust and of bread. She turned off the lamp, locked the door behind her for the last time, and posted the key through the bakery letterbox, as she had promised the baker she would. At the foot of the stairs Tilly was waiting with her coat on, and this time she said every sentimental thing that she had ever thought.

As the sun went down Marianne walked alone along the harbour wall, with her coat buttoned against the wind and the gulls settling on the rooftops for the night. Above her the Harbour Clock Tower stood square and steady, and as she reached the end of the quay its great bell began to strike the hour, slowly, and the hour was the right one. She stopped at the rail, and listened to every stroke until the last one had died away over the water, and she felt strangely glad.

She stood at the rail above the quiet water, near the head of the Fish Steps, and watched the last light fade from the sky and the first lamps come out along the quay. Her working life was over, she thought, and she felt the lightness of it and also the loss, the two of them side by side like old companions. But listening, she knew, was not a job that anyone could retire from, and it would go with her wherever she went.
